# Midterm project: PM2.5 and congestion pricing

New York City began charging most vehicles entering Manhattan's Congestion
Relief Zone (CRZ) on January 5, 2025. Did the odds of a high-PM2.5 day at CRZ
monitors change after the policy began, accounting for regional background
conditions? We define a high day relative to the pre-policy CRZ data; this is
a study-specific threshold, not a health standard.

This project builds on a published analysis of congestion pricing and air
quality [@fraser2025first] and extends its data through August 2026. Fraser et
al. analyze continuous daily PM2.5 using prediction-based counterfactuals; the
high-day outcome and segmented logistic model here are a separate course
analysis, not the paper's model. The analysis can show whether measurements
changed around the policy date. It cannot, by itself, show that
the toll caused a change. Weather, wildfire smoke, traffic, monitor operations,
and other events can affect PM2.5 at the same time. Your report must separate
the model's estimated association from a causal conclusion.

Use Python for this project. There is no restriction on which Python packages
you use. A grammar-of-graphics library such as `plotnine` is welcome.
Document the packages needed to reproduce your report.
Include executable Python code that reads the supplied CSV files from a local
`data/` folder, documents each cleaning choice, and produces the tables and
figures you discuss.

The instructor will provide two hourly CSV files covering June 1, 2023, through
August 31, 2026: [NYCCAS data](data/nyccas.csv) and [AirNow data](data/airnow.csv).
Keep them in a local `data/` folder next to your report. Do not include the raw
files in your submission.

- `nyccas.csv` contains readings from six NYCCAS monitors inside the
  CRZ, with location and site information.
- `airnow.csv` contains readings from four regional AirNow
  monitors used to estimate background PM2.5: Flemington, Rutgers University,
  Chester, and Paterson.

NYCCAS records are hourly averages, in micrograms per cubic meter, and the
`ObservationTimeUTC` field explicitly identifies UTC. AirNow’s `datetime`
field has no timezone offset in the CSV, but the AirNow hourly data
specification reports observation times in GMT (UTC). In both files, a
timestamp marks the beginning of its hour. The two files use different column
names and formats. Read the source descriptions and inspect the files before
deciding how to clean and combine them. AirNow may contain special or invalid
concentration codes; determine how to handle them from the values and
documentation. Do not treat a missing monitor reading as zero.

The data come from the NYC Community Air Survey (NYCCAS) archive
[@nyccasarchive] and the AirNow API [@airnowapi]. The AirNow hourly data
specification documents its GMT timestamp convention [@airnowhourly]. NYCCAS readings are preliminary and its
historical files can be revised. The accompanying [data README](data/README.md) explains which
source snapshots contribute to each period and documents NYCCAS correction
changes and records removed after sensor problems. Cite both data sources in
your report.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-pm25-clean}
Inspect and clean the hourly source files.

a. Describe the observational unit, time field and time zone, monitor key,
   PM2.5 value field, and units in each file.
b. Standardize the needed column names and parse timestamps as UTC. Check
   null values in each field, duplicate monitor-hour records, and missing
   hourly records between each monitor's first and last observations. Summarize
   valid observations and gaps by monitor and month. Distinguish null cells,
   absent monitor-hours, and periods before a monitor begins reporting.
c. Investigate unusual AirNow values, including negative codes. Identify
   codes that cannot be valid concentrations, document the exclusion rule,
   and keep the original files unchanged.
d. Apply the paper's strict range, $0 < PM_{2.5} < 25.5$ µg/m³, after
   removing invalid codes. Report retained and excluded counts, then repeat
   the main summary or model with all valid nonnegative values, including
   zeros and values at or above 25.5 µg/m³. Discuss what changes and whether
   high readings could be real events.
:::

::: {#exr-pm25-daily}
Create daily data and merge the sources.

a. Calculate daily maxima separately for each NYCCAS and AirNow monitor.
   Average the available AirNow monitor maxima for each date and report how
   many monitors contribute to each background estimate.
b. Create dates from the UTC timestamps. As a sensitivity check, convert
   timestamps to New York local time before creating dates; report which
   daily observations change and explain the difference.
c. Join date-level background estimates to NYCCAS monitor-days. Report row
   counts before and after the join, validate its cardinality, and explain
   how dates without background measurements are handled. Do not join the
   hourly files directly or replace missing measurements with zero.
d. Create a policy indicator that switches on January 5, 2025, and a variable
   counting days since that date. Retain January 2025 and explain how the
   intervention date determines these variables.
:::

::: {#exr-pm25-eda}
Explore and visualize the hourly and daily measurements.

a. Plot hourly-value distributions and daily maximum PM2.5 over time for
   each CRZ monitor. Mark January 5, 2025. Use a faceted plot to compare daily
   maxima across months and weekdays, then describe gaps, site differences,
   calendar patterns, and unusually high readings. Explain what the facets
   make easier to compare.
b. Plot the daily regional background series alongside the CRZ series.
   Compare the CRZ-minus-background difference before and after the policy
   date and explain why this raw contrast is descriptive.
c. Summarize how many AirNow monitors contribute to each daily background
   estimate and how many CRZ sites contribute over time. Explain why missing
   measurements are not zero-valued measurements.
d. Compare full-period trends with the primary range-filtered trends.
   Discuss how valid zeros and a few high readings can change daily-maximum
   summaries.
:::

::: {#exr-pm25-model}
Model high-PM2.5 days and interpret the results.

For each date, average the available CRZ monitor-specific daily maxima.
Define a high-PM2.5 day as a daily CRZ mean above the 75th percentile of
that measure before January 5, 2025. Calculate the cutoff using the primary
cleaned data, then keep it unchanged in the sensitivity analyses. This
study-specific cutoff is not a health standard. Report how many monitors
contribute on each date.

Your model must include a pre-policy time trend, an intervention level
change, a change in trend after the intervention, and the daily AirNow
regional background estimate. Fraser et al. use the square root of this
background estimate as a covariate in their predictive models; you may use
that transformation or justify another form. Choose any additional covariates
you consider useful. Define time in years from the start of the study, an
indicator that switches on January 5, 2025, and elapsed years since that date
(zero before the policy). A general form is

$$
\log\left(\frac{P(H_t=1)}{1-P(H_t=1)}\right)
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 t + \beta_2 T_t + \beta_3 D_t + g(X_t),
$$

where $H_t$ equals one when the CRZ daily mean exceeds the pre-policy 75th
percentile, $t$ is years since the study begins, $T_t$ is the intervention
indicator, and $D_t$ is years since the intervention (zero before it). The
function $g(X_t)$ must include the daily AirNow regional background estimate
and may include other covariates you choose to include.
The coefficient $\beta_2$ describes the immediate change in log odds at the
intervention date, and $\beta_3$ describes the change in the yearly log-odds
trend. Choose and construct any additional variables that help address
calendar patterns or regional conditions; explain their coding and why they
belong in your model. Possibilities include month, weekday, and weekend or
holiday status. AirNow is a regional background adjustment, not an untreated
comparison group.

a. Report the cutoff, high and non-high day counts, number of dates, and
monitor coverage. Fit your segmented model and report the intervention
level-change and trend-change estimates as odds ratios with 95% confidence
intervals. Explain how you constructed and chose any additional covariates.
Interpret estimates in terms of odds, not percentage-point changes in
probability.
b. Plot the observed high-day indicator and the model-predicted probability
over time. Compare pre-policy and post-policy patterns and state whether
the fitted change is concentrated at the policy date or accumulates as a
trend change.
c. Repeat the analysis using only the four monitors with data from the
start of the study period, then using all valid hourly observations without
the paper's range filter. Keep the primary cutoff fixed. Reconsider whether
your engineered covariates remain appropriate in each sensitivity analysis.
Compare estimates and describe how monitor coverage and data trimming affect
the result.
d. Check model fit and residual patterns over time. Explain why consecutive
daily outcomes may be dependent and how this affects usual standard errors
and confidence intervals. Explain why regional background is an adjustment
variable rather than an untreated comparison group. Consider the short
pre-policy record, weather, wildfire smoke, and changing monitor coverage;
conclude whether the results support a causal claim and distinguish an
estimated association from a causal effect.
:::

**Submission.**
Organize the report around these four steps. Include the Python code that
produces every reported result, and explain each cleaning and modeling choice.
Use ideas from chapters 1–9: reproducible projects, data checks, preparation,
EDA, visualization, and logistic-model interpretation.

Submit an independently written Quarto report to the Classroom 50 assignment.
Include your source code, selected tables and figures, cleaning decisions,
model output, and interpretation. Your report must run when the supplied CSV
files are placed in the expected local `data/` folder. Do not submit the raw
or cleaned data files.
